questions.q: Define a suspension and state the minimum particle size required for a mixture to be classified as one.
questions.a: A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles larger than 1000 nm (1 micron) are dispersed in a fluid medium. The particles are large enough to be visible under a microscope, settle on standing, and can be separated by filtration. A wrong answer (e.g., "particle size >1 nm") confuses suspensions with colloids, which have particles 1-1000 nm.

questions.q: You are given three mixtures: A (salt in water), B (milk in water), C (chalk powder in water). Which is a suspension? Justify using two properties.
questions.a: C (chalk powder in water) is a suspension. Justification: (1) Chalk particles are >1000 nm and settle at the bottom on standing. (2) Chalk can be separated by simple filtration using filter paper, leaving a residue. A is a true solution (particles <1 nm, no settling). B is a colloid (particles 1-1000 nm, shows Tyndall effect but does not settle). A wrong answer selecting B reveals confusion between colloids and suspensions based on cloudiness alone.

questions.q: A suspension of flour in water is left undisturbed for 30 minutes. Describe what happens and explain why.
questions.a: The flour particles gradually settle at the bottom of the container, and the upper layer of water becomes clearer. This happens because flour particles are >1000 nm and denser than water, so gravity overcomes the random Brownian motion that keeps smaller particles (in solutions and colloids) suspended. A wrong answer (e.g., "nothing happens, it stays uniform") reveals the misconception that all cloudy mixtures are stable like colloids.

questions.q: Compare a suspension and a colloid in terms of: (i) particle size, (ii) stability, (iii) filtration behavior, (iv) Tyndall effect. Present in a table.
questions.a:
| Property | Suspension | Colloid |
|---|---|---|
| Particle size | >1000 nm | 1-1000 nm |
| Stability | Unstable, particles settle | Stable, particles remain dispersed |
| Filtration | Separable by filter paper | Passes through filter paper |
| Tyndall effect | May show (particles large) | Shows strongly |
A wrong answer claiming colloids are filterable by ordinary filter paper reveals misunderstanding that filter paper pores (~1000 nm) trap suspension particles but let colloids pass.

questions.q: A student says: "If a mixture is cloudy, it must be a suspension." Evaluate with two counterexamples.
questions.a: The statement is false. Counterexample 1: Milk is cloudy but is a colloid (particle size 100-1000 nm), not a suspension — it does not settle on standing and passes through filter paper. Counterexample 2: Starch solution is cloudy but is a colloid — it shows Tyndall effect but does not settle and is not filterable. Cloudiness only indicates that particles are large enough to scatter light (>40 nm), which includes both colloids and suspensions. The distinguishing test is settling and filtration, not cloudiness. A wrong evaluation (agreeing) reveals reliance on visual appearance instead of particle size and stability criteria.

questions.q: Design an experiment to separate the components of a mixture containing salt, sand, and starch using only water, filter paper, a beaker, and a heat source. Explain the order of separation.
questions.a: Step 1: Add water to the mixture and stir. Salt dissolves (true solution), sand remains as suspension, starch forms a colloid. Step 2: Filter through filter paper. Sand (suspension, >1000 nm) is trapped as residue. Salt solution and starch colloid pass through as filtrate. Step 3: Heat the filtrate to evaporate water. Salt crystallises out (solid residue). Starch remains as a residue if heated to dryness. Order: sand first (filtration), then salt (evaporation), starch last (remaining solid). A poor design (e.g., filtering first without adding water) reveals inability to exploit solubility differences for sequential separation.
